text: Greenpeace found that a small number of the world's largest polluters, mostly outside Europe, are responsible for the overwhelming share of global emissions, and yet this Government continues to lecture ordinary Irish families about their carbon footprint while giving a free pass to the industries that matter most on the global stage. We are told to retrofit our homes, to change how we heat and travel, and I do not dispute that we all have a part to play, but the sacrifice being asked of ordinary people is wildly disproportionate to the sacrifice being asked of the corporations and countries that actually drive this crisis. Where is the ambition when it comes to holding multinational polluters to account? Where is the courage to challenge trading partners whose entire economic model depends on cheap, dirty energy? Instead we get carbon taxes dressed up as climate leadership, taxes that fall hardest on rural households, on people who have no public transport alternative, on families who cannot afford to retrofit a draughty house built forty years ago. That is not climate policy, it is a revenue-raising exercise with a green veneer. If the Government were serious, it would invest that revenue directly and visibly in retrofitting, in public transport, in supporting farmers to adopt sustainable practices, rather than allowing it to disappear into general expenditure. It would use its voice at European level to push for real accountability from the biggest emitters, not just for optics at climate summits. Irish people are not opposed to doing their part. What they resent, rightly, is being asked to carry a burden that should be shared far more broadly, while the Government congratulates itself for meeting targets on paper. We need honesty about where the emissions are actually coming from, and we need a policy that matches ambition with fairness.

I would ask the member opposite to visit some of these facilities, to speak with the workers whose lives have been changed by these investments, before he continues to characterize our record as one of inaction. I want to be clear that we are not simply importing last year's model without scrutiny. Lessons were learned from how calculated grades operated, and we are determined to apply them. At the same time, students need certainty as soon as we can responsibly provide it, because uncertainty itself is a significant driver of the anxiety Deputies have raised with me. I expect to be in a position to make a further announcement in the coming weeks once public health advice has been finalised, and I will ensure this House is kept informed as that process develops. I thank Deputies for their continued engagement on this issue, and I want to assure the students who are watching this debate that their wellbeing remains at the very centre of every decision being taken.

Faith-based organisations often have networks and relationships of trust that reach into communities where formal state institutions struggle to gain access, and that is an asset we should not overlook. They can also play a role in trauma counselling, in reintegration of former combatants, and in interfaith dialogue that addresses the sectarian dimensions of many conflicts. I have seen this work first-hand in visits to programmes supported by our development assistance, where local religious leaders have been instrumental in persuading armed groups to lay down weapons or in mediating disputes over land and resources that might otherwise have escalated into violence. It is precisely because these organisations are embedded in their communities, rather than parachuted in from outside, that their interventions can carry a legitimacy that other actors sometimes lack. That said, I want to be careful not to suggest that peacebuilding can simply be outsourced to civil society. Government has a central responsibility to create the political and security conditions in which reconciliation can take root, and faith-based organisations work most effectively when they are supported by, rather than substituted for, a coherent state strategy. We should also be alert to the risk that in some contexts religious institutions have themselves been implicated in division rather than reconciliation, so partnership needs to be built on careful assessment of who genuinely commands trust across communal lines. My Department will continue to fund programmes that bring these organisations into structured partnership with local government and international agencies, and I would welcome further engagement from hon. Members on how we can strengthen that framework going forward.

I raise this not because I believe the House should spend its time entertaining fantastical claims to the throne, but because Mr Hallett's case illustrates something more troubling: the ease with which conspiracy theories can now spread and attract genuine followings, however threadbare the underlying evidence. Mr Hallett has, over the years, gathered a small but devoted online following, and has used various platforms to solicit funds from supporters who apparently believe his claims. This is not a harmless eccentricity. Vulnerable people have handed over money on the strength of assurances that cannot withstand the mildest historical scrutiny. Genealogists and constitutional historians who have examined the claim in detail have found nothing to support it, and the College of Arms has, on the rare occasions it has been asked, dismissed it outright. I mention this case alongside several others precisely because it sits on a spectrum with more consequential forms of misinformation that this House has debated at length, from health disinformation to claims about the legitimacy of elections. The mechanisms are the same: a grievance narrative, a charismatic figure willing to exploit it, and a digital environment that rewards engagement over accuracy. I do not think it is the role of this House to adjudicate genealogical disputes, but I do think we have a responsibility to ask what protections exist for people who are persuaded to part with their savings on the strength of claims like these, and whether our consumer protection and fraud legislation is keeping pace with the way such schemes now operate online. I would welcome the Minister's view on whether existing powers are adequate to that task.

My colleague raises a fair point when he says the word has become something of a rhetorical shield, deployed in speeches and press releases without the substance that would give it weight. Reconciliation cannot simply mean an apology issued once and then set aside. It has to mean structural change: land claims resolved rather than litigated indefinitely, clean drinking water delivered on every reserve rather than promised in successive budgets, and a justice system that stops overrepresenting Indigenous peoples in our prisons. This bill takes a step in the right direction, but I want to be honest with the House that a single piece of legislation, however well intentioned, cannot carry the full weight of what reconciliation demands. We need sustained, multi-generational commitment across every department of government, and frankly across every party represented here, because Indigenous communities have watched governments of every stripe make promises that outlasted the news cycle but not much longer. What gives me some hope is that the conversation in this chamber has shifted. Members on all sides now speak with more fluency about the history of residential schools, about the Indian Act's ongoing legacy, about the specific claims process, than they did even a decade ago. That shift matters, but only if it translates into votes, into funding decisions, and into a willingness to cede jurisdiction where Indigenous governments are asking for it. I look forward to continuing this debate as the bill proceeds through committee.

When a decision is made that shocks the conscience of the nation, as the transfer in the McClintic case did, it is entirely appropriate for parliamentarians to ask hard questions and to demand that the responsible Minister explain what safeguards exist to prevent it from happening again. Victims' families do not get a second chance to see justice done. They live with the consequences of these decisions for the rest of their lives, often reliving their trauma every time a parole hearing or a transfer decision makes headlines. I would ask the government to commit today to a full review of the policies governing offender placement, and to ensure that victims and their families have a meaningful voice in that process, not an afterthought consultation after the decision has already been made.

For too long, local councillors, who are closest to their communities and who understand the particular pressures facing them, have been treated as little more than administrators implementing decisions made elsewhere. This Bill begins to redress that balance, and I would encourage the Minister to go further in subsequent legislation. We should be looking at giving local authorities greater revenue-raising powers, so that they are not permanently dependent on central government allocations that can be cut or delayed at short notice. We should also be looking at how we can strengthen the capacity of local authorities to deliver housing directly, rather than relying so heavily on the private market to meet demand that it consistently fails to meet. I have seen in my own constituency how effective local authorities can be when they are given the resources and the authority to act, whether that is in regenerating town centres, delivering social housing, or supporting local enterprise. What has been missing is not capability but confidence, on the part of central government, to trust local authorities with real power. I hope this Bill marks the beginning of a more durable shift in that direction, and I look forward to scrutinising its provisions in more detail as it progresses through committee.

I want to put on record my thanks to RICS for the constructive and detailed nature of that engagement, because it strengthened the final drafting considerably. Their concern, as I understood it, centred on ensuring that arbitrators could not be removed on spurious or vexatious grounds that would undermine the independence which is fundamental to the arbitration process. We listened carefully to that concern and amended the relevant clause to introduce a clearer threshold, requiring evidence of misconduct or incapacity rather than simple disagreement with an arbitrator's determination. I think that strikes the right balance between accountability and independence, and I am grateful to noble Lords in the other place for pressing us on this point, because the Bill is undoubtedly stronger for it. We also took on board feedback regarding the transitional arrangements for arbitrations already underway at the point of commencement, ensuring that ongoing proceedings are not disrupted by a change in the applicable rules partway through. This is a technical but important safeguard, and one that several stakeholders, including practising arbitrators themselves, specifically requested. I would note more generally that this Bill has benefited enormously from the willingness of professional bodies to engage constructively with government throughout its passage, rather than simply lobbying from the sidelines. That kind of engagement produces better legislation, and I hope it is a model we continue to follow as further reforms to our arbitration and dispute resolution framework are brought forward in future sessions. I commend the Bill, as amended, to the House, and I look forward to hearing further contributions from hon. and right hon. Members.

I would ask the Taoiseach today to clarify, in specific terms, what timeline his Government is now working to, whether draft legislation will be published before the end of this term, and whether he can commit to genuine powers being attached to these offices rather than a hollowed-out version designed simply to generate a positive headline. These are not throwaway remarks from a minor official. They come from the man who controls Russia's nuclear arsenal and who has already demonstrated, through the illegal annexation of Crimea and the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, that he is prepared to act on this revanchist worldview with military force. This House must be clear-eyed about what we are dealing with. This is not a leader who can be reasoned with through appeasement, nor one who will be satisfied by territorial concessions dressed up as a peace settlement. Every time the West has offered concessions in the hope of moderating his behaviour, from the muted response to Georgia in 2008 to the limited sanctions following Crimea in 2014, we have seen that restraint interpreted not as goodwill but as weakness, and it has emboldened further aggression. That is why our continued support for Ukraine, in military, economic, and diplomatic terms, cannot waver, regardless of how long this conflict continues or how difficult the winter ahead may be for energy prices here at home. I understand the pressures that constituents are facing, and I do not dismiss them, but I would ask this House to remember that the alternative to sustained support is a Europe where borders can once again be redrawn by force, where sovereign nations can be swallowed by their larger neighbours, and where the rules-based international order that has underpinned our peace and prosperity for decades is allowed to collapse. We owe it to Ukraine, and frankly to ourselves, to see this through.

This is not a marginal problem confined to a handful of exploitative employers. It runs through entire sectors of our economy, from delivery and courier services to social care, and it leaves hundreds of thousands of workers without access to sick pay, holiday entitlement, pension contributions, or protection against unfair dismissal. The Taylor review itself, commissioned by this Government, was unambiguous in identifying the problem, and yet three years on we are still waiting for the promised Employment Bill that would turn those recommendations into enforceable law. That delay is not an accident. It reflects a Government that talks about levelling up and protecting workers while consistently prioritising the interests of employers who benefit from the status quo. Labour's position is straightforward: we would introduce a single status of worker for all but the genuinely self-employed, closing the loopholes that allow bogus self-employment to flourish, and we would establish a single enforcement body with real teeth to ensure that rights on paper translate into rights in practice. We would also address the tax distortions that the Deputy has rightly identified, ensuring that the system does not create a perverse incentive for employers to misclassify workers simply to reduce their national insurance liabilities. Working people across this country deserve security, not the constant anxiety of not knowing whether they will be offered shifts next week, and this Government's continued inaction is a betrayal of the promises it made when the Taylor review was first published.

Housing delivery has fallen far short of what was promised for far too many years, and the gap between announcement and completion has become one of the defining failures of governance in this State. We can publish targets, we can launch new schemes with new acronyms, but none of that matters to a family sleeping in emergency accommodation tonight, or to a young couple who have given up hope of ever owning their own home because prices have risen faster than their wages ever could. I recognise the scale of the challenge is significant. Land activation, planning delays, construction cost inflation, and a shortage of skilled labour in the sector all present genuine obstacles, and I do not pretend there is a simple fix. But acknowledging complexity is not the same as accepting failure, and I believe this Government has too often used complexity as an excuse rather than a spur to action. What we need now is relentless focus on delivery: local authorities empowered and resourced to build directly, rather than relying so heavily on the private market; a serious effort to bring vacant and derelict properties back into use, of which there are thousands across this country; and a State construction capacity that can step in where the market fails to deliver at the pace and scale required. We also need to be honest that some of the schemes introduced in recent years, however well intentioned, have contributed to house price inflation rather than affordability. Trust in this State's ability to deliver on housing has been badly eroded, and it will only be rebuilt through consistent, visible progress, not through further announcements. That is the standard by which this Government should be judged, and it is the standard I intend to hold it to.

The Malthouse compromise, for those unfamiliar with its details, sought to combine the existing withdrawal agreement's financial settlement and citizens' rights provisions with a technological solution to the Northern Ireland border question, avoiding the backstop entirely by relying on trusted trader schemes and mutual recognition arrangements that already exist in other contexts around the world. I recognise that some colleagues on both sides of this debate have dismissed such technological solutions as unproven or unrealistic within the available timeframe, but I would gently point out that similar mechanisms already operate successfully on other borders, and dismissing them out of hand does not strike me as the pragmatic approach this moment demands. My constituents did not vote to leave the European Union so that we could remain indefinitely tied to its regulatory orbit through a backstop with no unilateral exit mechanism. Nor did they vote to see our fishing industry, our agricultural sector, or our ability to strike independent trade deals permanently constrained by arrangements negotiated, in some cases, before we had even left. What they want, and what I believe this House owes them, is a departure that honours the result of the referendum while protecting the Good Friday Agreement and the integrity of the United Kingdom's internal market. I believe the compromise before us achieves that balance better than the alternatives currently on offer, and I would urge colleagues across this House, whatever their views on the merits of Brexit itself, to engage constructively with a solution that offers a genuine way through this impasse rather than perpetuating the paralysis that has characterised recent months.

I do not say this to relitigate the entirety of the Iraq war in this Chamber, a task that would occupy considerably more time than is available to me this afternoon, but I raise it because it speaks to a broader pattern that concerns me deeply: the tendency of those who held office at the time of consequential decisions to revise their accounts once the political and human costs of those decisions have become fully apparent. Chilcot was thorough, it was exhaustive, and it reached conclusions that were uncomfortable for many who served in government at the time, myself included in terms of my party's historical position. Those conclusions should not now be quietly set aside because they are inconvenient. I would ask the House to reflect on what lessons we have genuinely internalised from that period, because the temptation to intervene militarily on the basis of intelligence that later proves flawed or politically shaped has not disappeared from our political culture. We see echoes of the same pressures in debates about intervention elsewhere, and I believe this House owes it to the service personnel who lost their lives, and to the countless Iraqi civilians whose lives were upended, to maintain a rigorous and honest reckoning with what went wrong, rather than allowing the passage of time to soften judgments that were reached only after painstaking and exhaustive inquiry.

What we have seen in practice is that the scheme has been most heavily utilised in areas where house prices are already elevated, effectively subsidising demand in precisely the markets where supply constraints are most acute. This is a fairly predictable outcome when you introduce a demand-side measure without a corresponding and sufficiently ambitious supply-side response. I am not opposed to the principle of supporting first-time buyers; indeed, I think there is a strong case for well-designed interventions that help people onto the property ladder. But the evidence from the Economic and Social Research Institute and others has consistently pointed to help-to-buy contributing to upward pressure on new-build prices in exactly the areas where affordability is already most stretched, which somewhat defeats the purpose. I would also note that the scheme has done relatively little for buyers in lower-income brackets, who often cannot afford new-build properties even with the assistance the scheme provides, and who are effectively excluded from its benefits by virtue of where they can afford to live. If we are serious about improving affordability rather than simply increasing the number of transactions taking place, we need to look much more critically at how this scheme interacts with planning policy, with cost-rental delivery, and with the broader supply pipeline. I would ask the Minister to commit to a full, independent review of the scheme's distributional effects before any further extension is considered, because continuing a policy simply because it is popular with those who benefit from it is not the same as continuing a policy because it works.

This Bill matters because it addresses a gap that has existed for far too long in how we regulate trade with, and investment in, territories recognised as illegally occupied under international law. Ireland has consistently, at the level of rhetoric, condemned the settlement enterprise in the Occupied Palestinian Territories as illegal and as a fundamental obstacle to peace, and yet our trading relationships have not always reflected that stated position with the consistency one might expect. I recognise that this is a Bill that has attracted significant international attention, and not a small amount of pressure from various quarters urging its rejection. I would say to those who have raised concerns that Ireland is not seeking to single out any one conflict or any one people; the principle at stake is a general one, rooted in international humanitarian law, regarding the illegality of settlement activity in occupied territory under the Fourth Geneva Convention. If this principle is worth stating in our foreign policy, it is worth reflecting in our trade and procurement law as well. I find it difficult to understand the logic of a policy that leaves people in limbo for months or, all too often, years, unable to work, unable to contribute, unable to build any sense of purpose or independence, and then wonders why integration outcomes for those eventually granted status are not as strong as they could be. I have met asylum seekers in my own constituency who were doctors, engineers, and teachers in their home countries, desperate to contribute their skills to this country while their claims are processed, and instead forced into enforced idleness that serves no one's interests, least of all the taxpayer who is asked to fund their support in the meantime. The right to work after a reasonable period, say six months, is not a radical proposition; it is the position adopted by many of our European neighbours, and I would urge the Government to look again at the evidence rather than relying on assumptions about disincentive effects that the data simply does not support.

As currently drafted, the penalties available to the courts for offences involving the illegal hunting, trapping, or trade of protected species are, frankly, derisory when weighed against the profits that can be made from wildlife crime, whether that involves the illegal taking of protected birds of prey, the destruction of protected habitats, or trafficking in endangered species and their derivatives. Enforcement officers within the National Parks and Wildlife Service have told us directly that the current penalty structure provides almost no deterrent effect, particularly for organised operations that can absorb a modest fine as simply a cost of doing business. Trump has, over many years, waged an open campaign against journalists and news organisations he deems unfavourable to him, labelling legitimate reporting as fake news and encouraging his supporters to view the free press with suspicion and hostility rather than as an essential pillar of democratic accountability. For the Taoiseach to express even qualified sympathy with that worldview should trouble every Member of this House who values a free and independent press as fundamental to a functioning democracy. Media plurality is not an abstract policy concern; it is the mechanism by which citizens in a democracy hold power to account, by which corruption is exposed, by which government decisions are scrutinised beyond the confines of this Chamber. When political leaders, anywhere in the world, begin to characterise inconvenient journalism as illegitimate rather than simply disagreeing with its conclusions, they undermine public trust in institutions that democracy fundamentally depends upon. I would ask the Taoiseach to clarify precisely what he meant by his remarks, because if he was simply making a diplomatic pleasantry in the context of a bilateral relationship, that is one thing, but if he genuinely holds sympathy for a view of the media as an adversary to be delegitimised rather than a check on power to be respected, that is an entirely different and far more troubling matter. This House, and the Irish public, deserve absolute clarity on where the Taoiseach genuinely stands on the fundamental importance of a free press, particularly at a moment when press freedom is under sustained pressure in democracies around the world, including some of our closest allies.

Marcuse argued that a society which permits the expression of all viewpoints equally, without regard to their relative power or their capacity to cause harm, in fact entrenches existing structures of oppression by treating dominant and marginalised voices as though they occupy an equal playing field. It is a seductive argument in certain respects, and I understand why it continues to resonate with some contemporary student activists who invoke similar logic when arguing for the no-platforming of speakers whose views they find objectionable. But I believe it is, ultimately, a deeply illiberal argument dressed in the language of liberation, because it requires someone, inevitably an institution or an individual in a position of authority, to determine which viewpoints are sufficiently dominant or harmful to warrant suppression, and history offers no shortage of examples of that power being abused, often against the very marginalised voices such restrictions claim to protect. Universities exist, at their best, as spaces where difficult and uncomfortable ideas can be tested, challenged, and, where they are found wanting, refuted through argument and evidence, rather than through administrative suppression. I would rather see a genuinely Marcusean argument defeated in open debate, exposed for its flaws through rigorous engagement, than see it, or any other contested idea, banished from campus discourse by university administrators anxious to avoid controversy. That is the tradition of free inquiry our universities were built upon, and it is a tradition worth defending, even against ideas, like Marcuse's, that some in this House and beyond find genuinely persuasive.

Restoring the institutions is not, and should never be treated as, an end in itself; it must be accompanied by genuine, functioning government that can address the very real challenges facing people in Northern Ireland, from the longest health waiting lists in these islands to the cost of living pressures that are being felt as acutely there as anywhere else in the United Kingdom. I would say to those parties currently engaged in these talks that the people of Northern Ireland have shown extraordinary patience through repeated periods of political instability over the past quarter century, but that patience is not infinite, and every additional month without a functioning Executive is a month in which decisions that require democratic accountability are instead left to civil servants operating without a mandate to make the kind of strategic choices that Northern Ireland urgently needs. I remain hopeful, based on the constructive tone of recent engagement, that we can reach a resolution that allows the institutions to be restored on a sustainable basis, rather than simply papering over the underlying tensions that led to their collapse in the first place. This Government will continue to act as a facilitator and guarantor of the Good Friday Agreement in all its parts, working with the Irish Government where appropriate under the terms of that Agreement, and I will keep this House updated as these talks progress, because Members across this Chamber have a legitimate interest in seeing devolved government restored and functioning effectively in Northern Ireland.

I would ask the Minister to confirm, specifically, what stage the project has now reached in terms of design, planning permission, and procurement, and whether a firm construction start date has been agreed with the relevant capital planning unit within the HSE. I would also ask whether lessons have genuinely been learned from the previous delay, and what specific governance arrangements are now in place to ensure that if problems arise during delivery, they are identified and communicated to this House and to the affected community promptly, rather than allowed to fester silently until the delay becomes impossible to ignore. This community has waited long enough, and I do not think it is unreasonable to ask for the kind of transparency and accountability that would allow genuine confidence to be restored.

Sergeant Ratana had served with the Metropolitan Police for many years, and by all accounts was a dedicated and well-respected officer who was simply doing his job, protecting the public, when his life was so cruelly taken from him. My thoughts, and I know the thoughts of every Member of this House, are with his family, his partner, and his colleagues at Croydon custody centre, who now have to carry on their vital work while grieving the loss of a friend and colleague under the most traumatic of circumstances. This tragedy should prompt this House to reflect seriously on the safety of officers working in custody suites and other high-risk environments, where the potential for violent confrontation is ever present, often with individuals who are in crisis, under the influence of drugs, or in possession of weapons that officers may not be aware of until the moment of greatest danger. I would ask the Minister what specific review is being undertaken into the circumstances of this incident, including whether existing search and safety protocols within custody settings are adequate, and whether additional protective equipment or procedural changes are needed to reduce the risk of similar incidents occurring in future. We ask a great deal of our police officers, and incidents like this are a stark reminder that the risks they face are not abstract or occasional, but a constant feature of the job they do to keep the rest of us safe. This House owes it to Sergeant Ratana's memory, and to every serving officer, to ensure that every reasonable step is taken to protect them while they protect us.

Genuine legacy means the young people who volunteered, who worked in hospitality, in security, in event management, in broadcasting, and in a dozen other disciplines during this programme, carrying those skills forward into sustainable careers, rather than a temporary surge in employment that evaporates the moment the final event concludes. I have seen, in previous major events hosted in this country and elsewhere, both the promise and the pitfalls of legacy planning. Done well, it can transform the economic prospects of a region for a generation, embedding new skills, new infrastructure, and renewed civic pride that outlasts the event itself by decades. Done poorly, it leaves behind expensive facilities with no sustainable use, a temporary bump in employment statistics that fades within a year or two, and a lingering sense among local communities that they hosted something extraordinary but were left with little of lasting value to show for it. I would ask the Minister what specific, measurable targets have been set for skills legacy from this programme, including how many participants are expected to move into sustained employment within the relevant sectors, and what mechanism will be used to track those outcomes over the coming years, not simply in the immediate aftermath when political attention is highest, but over a five or ten year horizon that would allow us to properly assess whether the legacy promises made at the outset of this programme were actually delivered, or whether they proved, as legacy promises so often do, more durable in speeches than in practice.
